# 5. Interaction Flow Based on the above functional architecture and the integration model of Agent/Copilot, this chapter focuses on how to achieve end-to-end processing of both single-domain autonomy and cross-domain collaborative fault scenarios through the interaction and cooperation of agents at the Resource layer and the Service layer. ## 5.1. Fault Management Overall Flow [Figure: Figure 3. Full workflow of AN L4 fault management: Single Domain + Cross Domain] For single-domain fault [Red 1 → 2 → 3]: Fault agents in a single domain automatically identify, diagnose, and handle faults. The agent self-closed-loop mode and Copilot H5 plug-in/LPI integration mode are used. For cross-domain faults [blue 1→2a/2b→3→4→5]: Based on incident data reported by single-domain agents, cross-domain agents proactively identify faults and drive the faults by upper-layer/external systems (such as service assurance or complaint-driven). Cross-domain fault agents automatically analyze and demarcate faults, and work with single-domain agents to automatically locate and rectify faults. The agent-based diagnosis mode and Copilot H5 plug-in/LPI integration mode are used. This document only introduces the general fault management process and the cross-domain fault management process. The single-domain fault management process is specifically described in IG1501A-X. ## 5.2. Cross-Domain Fault Management Flow This section uses the scenario where wireless base stations are out of service in batches due to IP network line disconnection as an example. The E2E process is described as follows: [Figure: Cross-domain fault management flow for batch wireless base station outage due to IP network line disconnection] Step 1-2: represent the fault occurrence phase. As above example, in the IP network AN domain, a line interruption fault occurs. In the mobile network AN domain, a mass base station outage fault occurs. Steps 3-4 represent the fault awareness phase. For example, in the above figure, the service layer fault agent receives various types of information, including (3a) incident actively sent by the mobile network agent, (3b) incident actively sent by the IP network agent, and (3c) user complaints. The service layer cross-domain agent performs cross-domain correlation analysis on this information (4). Step 5 is the analysis and decision phase of fault management. In the above example, the service layer cross-domain identifies the fault as a cross-domain fault and determines the site where the fault occurred and the return link. It then sends diagnostic information to the corresponding resource layer fault agent (IP network fault agent). The resource layer fault agent performs self-diagnosis and returns the fault information and handling recommendations to the cross-domain agent. Steps 6-8 represent the execution and repair phase of fault management. In the above example, the cross-domain agent receives fault information and repair suggestions sent by the resource layer agent and determines that automatic repair is not possible, prompting the initiation of a work order system to assign the repair work order to the FME (6). The FME interacts with the service layer’s FME Copilot through an app to query relevant information about the faulty device (7). The service layer FME Copilot collaborates with the resource layer FME Copilot, which provides the FME with natural language-based operational guidance to assist in completing the fault repair (8). ## 5.3.
